verses.text: Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, after the abominations of the nations whom Yahweh cast out before the children of Israel.

For he built again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he raised up altars for Baal, and made an Asherah, as Ahab king of Israel did, and worshiped all the army of the sky, and served them.
He built altars in Yahweh’s house, of which Yahweh said, “I will put my name in Jerusalem.”
He built altars for all the army of the sky in the two courts of Yahweh’s house.

He made his son to pass through the fire, practiced sorcery, used enchantments, and dealt with those who had familiar spirits, and with wizards. He did much evil in Yahweh’s sight, to provoke him to anger.

He set the engraved image of Asherah that he had made in the house of which Yahweh said to David and to Solomon his son, “In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name forever;

I will not cause the feet of Israel to wander any more out of the land which I gave their fathers, if only they will observe to do according to all that I have commanded them, and according to all the law that my servant Moses commanded them.”
But they didn’t listen, and Manasseh seduced them to do that which is evil more than the nations did whom Yahweh destroyed before the children of Israel.
Yahweh spoke by his servants the prophets, saying,
“Because Manasseh king of Judah has done these abominations, and has done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, who were before him, and has also made Judah to sin with his idols;
therefore Yahweh the God of Israel says, ‘Behold, I bring such evil on Jerusalem and Judah that whoever hears of it, both his ears will tingle.
I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of Ahab’s house; and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down.
I will cast off the remnant of my inheritance, and deliver them into the hands of their enemies. They will become a prey and a plunder to all their enemies,
because they have done that which is evil in my sight, and have provoked me to anger, since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day.’”

Moreover Manasseh shed innocent blood very much, until he had filled Jerusalem from one end to another; besides his sin with which he made Judah to sin, in doing that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight.
Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and all that he did, and his sin that he sinned, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Manasseh slept with his fathers, and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza; and Amon his son reigned in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Meshullemeth the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, as Manasseh his father did.
He walked in all the ways that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshiped them;
and he abandoned Yahweh, the God of his fathers, and didn’t walk in the way of Yahweh.
The servants of Amon conspired against him, and put the king to death in his own house.
But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against king Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
Now the rest of the acts of Amon which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Manasseh ascends at twelve—a boy with a crown and the whole kingdom in his hands. His mother Hephzibah's name means 'my delight is in her,' yet her son will become Judah's greatest heartbreaker. Sometimes the young are given too much too soon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evil in Yahweh's sight—this phrasing appears when a king chooses idolatry after knowing better. Manasseh had grown up watching his father Hezekiah trust the Lord and live. The choice to turn away is always someone's decision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He undoes his father's reforms—tears down the high places Hezekiah fought to remove. The weight of undoing goodness is a peculiar pain. He doesn't just drift; he actively reverses the path, choosing Baal and the sky-gods his father rejected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He builds altars to Yahweh in the Lord's own house, even as he desecrates it. This is the deepest corruption—not honest rejection, but counterfeit worship, mixing truth with lies in the very place God promised His name. The Lord's house becomes a stage for pretense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In both courts of the Lord's house he raises altars to the 'army of the sky'—filling sacred space with idolatry as if to drown out the voice of the God who made the heavens themselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He makes his son pass through fire—the horror of child sacrifice. This verse names the depth of Manasseh's rebellion: he doesn't just turn from God; he turns his own child into a burnt offering to demons. The measure of a heart is how it treats the helpless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The engraved Asherah image he places in God's house is a deliberate desecration of the covenant house itself. God had promised His name would dwell there forever—and Manasseh answers by setting up an idol where the Lord's name should reign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The promise is clear: obey the law, and Israel will dwell safely in the land forever. Manasseh ignores it. He knows the condition; he chooses the curse instead. Freedom demands we be real about the cost of our rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He seduces the nation—not merely leads them astray, but actively persuades them to evil 'more than the nations' God destroyed. A king's corruption spreads like rot; it infects those under his rule, and they become complicit in his rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophets speak. Even in the face of Manasseh's rebellion, God sends His servants to warn. The Lord does not leave His people without witness, even when they refuse to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His abominations exceed even the Amorites who came before—a chilling indictment. Manasseh doesn't just fall short; he sinks lower than those God judged for their wickedness. And he drags Judah down with him through his idols.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Whoever hears of it, both his ears will tingle'—this is the sound of judgment so terrible that the mere telling of it shocks. The Lord's patience has limits, and when He speaks judgment, all heaven and earth take notice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The line of Samaria and plummet of Ahab's house—measuring tools turned to destruction. Just as the builders measured Samaria's fall, so the Lord will measure Jerusalem's. The city that knew the Lord's name will be wiped clean like a dirty dish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The remnant of His inheritance cast off, delivered into enemy hands—yet even in this darkness, He calls them 'my inheritance.' Judgment, not abandonment. A father may discipline, but He does not disown His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They provoked Him 'since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day'—a long history of turning away. Generations of rebellion accumulate; the Lord's patience, though long, is not endless. Consequences catch up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He fills Jerusalem with innocent blood 'from one end to another'—the brutality is totalizing, systematic. This is not mere policy disagreement; this is state terror. Yet even so, God sees each victim and their blood cries out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A formula: 'the rest of his acts' are recorded elsewhere. Even the king's full record—his accomplishments, his strategies—are noted but deemed insufficient for the living chronicle. His legacy is his rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sleeps with his fathers and is buried in a garden—not the royal tomb, but a private grave. Even in death, there is a hint of shame. The garden of Uzza becomes his last resting place, unmarked by glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon, his son, ascends at twenty-two and reigns only two years. His mother is Meshullemeth. The line continues, but the pattern repeats—another boy-king, another descent into evil. One generation does not break the cycle of rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon walks in his father's ways—this is the tragedy of inheritance without redemption. He does not learn from Manasseh's judgment; he copies it, as if evil were a birthright to be claimed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He serves the idols his father served—not his own twisted invention, but a dutiful repetition of his father's sin. Some of the deepest wounds come not from rebellion, but from loyal sons who inherit their fathers' darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He abandons Yahweh, 'the God of his fathers.' These words are a reversal—the God of his fathers is set aside as if He were an old habit. Amon prefers the false gods, and with that choice, breaks the covenant his people once knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His own servants conspire and kill him in his own house—not in battle, but in the privacy of his dwelling. A king surrounded by those he trusts becomes vulnerable to those he has wronged or alienated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people of the land rise up and make Josiah king—and here the darkness breaks. Out of two evil reigns comes a child who will seek the Lord. God plants hope even in the rubble of human sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again the formula: his acts are written elsewhere. But Amon's reign is so brief, so empty of consequence except his death, that even the chroniclers seem to hurry past it. Some lives leave little but a shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He is buried in Uzza's garden—the same garden where Manasseh rests. Readers today hear an echo: evil fathers and rebellious sons lie together in unmarked ground, while the young man raised in their shadow rises to seek the Lord. Grace breaks the pattern.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
